name: Mickey Minnie Playschool
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Designed for admin, used by parent: Every flow assumed an admin user. Parents had to navigate seventeen screens to find a single piece of information. | WhatsApp was winning: Parents stayed on WhatsApp because it was faster. The app had to feel as fast as a message, not as slow as a portal. | Pickup-line UX: The app's heaviest use happens one-handed, in a car, at 2:50pm. The product had to be designed for that exact moment. | Four campuses, one app: Each campus had different schedules, fee structures, and teachers. The product couldn't fragment by location.
strategy: One screen, three answers: The parent home shows today's update, today's pickup time, and today's fee status. Three answers, no taps. | Faster than WhatsApp: Every common action — pay, view, message teacher — takes under fifteen seconds. The app has to outrun the chat group. | Big targets, low-light: All tap targets sized for one-handed use in low light. The app is opened in cars, not at desks. | Joyful, not childish: Bright primary colour palette. Playful illustration. The brand is for the kid; the UX is for the adult.
solution: Design for the moments that matter, from the classroom to the playground.

results.label: of all app opens happen in a 45-minute window — pickup.
median time from app-open to today's-update glance — down from 38s.
one product, four configurations. No fragmentation.
active families using the app daily after redesign.

quote.text: Build a brand for the children, but make it resonate with the parents.
quote.author: Mickey Minnie Playschool

headline: A playful rebrand for a beloved playschool.

name: Zestee
subtitle: ui-ux case study
problem: Three locations, three brands: Each café had been opened in a hurry. Every signboard, takeaway cup, and Instagram grid told a slightly different story. | Mistaken for a juice bar: Drop-in customers ordered juice and left. The coffee program — the actual business — was invisible from the street. | Forgotten on Instagram: No one geo-tagged Zestee. The interiors were beautiful but the brand never asked to be photographed. | No system, no scale: Opening café four would mean rebuilding café one from scratch. There was no kit of parts to copy.
strategy: Warmth, not luxury: Terracotta and cream beat black and gold. Zestee should feel like a friend's living room, not a hotel lobby. | Hand over machine: Hand-painted signage. Hand-stamped sleeves. The brand wears its making process. | Type-led: A single custom display face does the heavy lifting. No stock fonts, no decorative flourish. | Photographable: Every cup, plate, and sticker is designed first as a flat-lay. The brand earns its Instagram.
solution: Built to be photographed. Designed to be returned to.

average ticket size — 1.8× the neighbourhood average.

name: Vanya Luxe
subtitle: ui-ux case study
problem: Balancing Act: The brand needed to communicate clinical science without looking like medicine. | Tactile Digital: How do you convey the texture of a luxury cream through a website? | Information Hierarchy: Customers need to know active ingredients, but too much text breaks the luxury aesthetic. | Packaging Constraints: Sustainable materials had to feel heavy and premium.
strategy: Whitespace as Luxury: Letting the products breathe on the page. | Macro Photography: Showing the exact texture of the product. | Clear Typography: Elegant serifs paired with highly legible sans-serifs for ingredients. | Frictionless UX: A checkout process that feels effortless.
solution: Vanya Luxe brings clinical efficacy to the luxury skincare space. We created a digital experience and packaging system that feels as refined as the formulas themselves.

name: PIQ
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Energy drinks look like energy drinks: The category is a wall of black cans and neon angles. Hard to stand out by joining the chorus. | Lemonade looks like a kids' drink: Pastel pink, hand-drawn lemons, summer-camp lettering. Not the brief either. | Three formats, one face: A can, a glass bottle, and a squeeze pouch — each one wants to look like a different brand by default. | Caffeine credibility: The brand has to whisper 'this works' without writing it on the can in screaming yellow.
strategy: Lemon-first colour: The brand's green is the colour of an under-ripe lemon — not the cliché yellow. | Confident type, no shouting: A single condensed sans does all the typography. No display flourishes, no italics. | Photography over illustration: Every brand asset is a real product, real ice, real water. The drink earns its photo. | Format-modular: Can, bottle, squeeze — same wordmark, same proportion, three completely different containers.
solution: Lemon. Caffeine. An exclamation mark — earned, not added.

sugar — a third of the category baseline.

name: The Ube Press
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Trend vs. heritage: Most ube products lean into the Instagram colour. The Reyeses wanted heritage credibility, not a viral moment. | The flavour syrup problem: Ninety percent of Western ube products are syrup-flavoured. The Ube Press uses the real root. The brand has to make that obvious. | Two markets, one face: Filipino diaspora customers and curious-Western customers want different stories. The brand has to be both. | Purple is loud: Ube's natural colour is non-negotiable. The brand has to wear it without becoming cartoonish.
strategy: Single colour, single hero: The whole brand is built around one ube purple. Every other element is restrained to let it lead. | Tagalog as first language: The wordmark includes a Tagalog tagline. The diaspora reads it first; everyone else reads it next. | Hand over machine: Hand-drawn label illustrations, hand-stamped batch numbers. The brand wears its labour. | Root, not flavour: Every label calls out the farm. The product's truth is the brand's strategy.
solution: Real root. Real hands. A real grandmother somewhere in Bohol.

results.label: of new buyers tried The Ube Press because they recognised the wordmark on a shelf, not from an ad.
average bottle price — positioned at premium juice tier.
single-origin sourcing from four Bohol cooperatives.
real root, cold-pressed, no flavouring.

name: GlobeTap
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Opened on holidays, ignored on Tuesdays: Users only thought about Globetap when travelling. The product was a holiday utility, not a daily one. | Stations without context: The map showed stations. It didn't show whether one was on your usual route, or whether it would save you time. | No reason to return: The product had no progress, no streak, no signal that using it mattered. | Onboarding was a search bar: Day-one users were dropped onto a map and told to figure it out. 60% never came back.
strategy: Bottle-first: The first screen isn't a map — it's a bottle. The product starts where the behaviour starts. | Route-aware: Stations are filtered against the user's actual commute, not the radius around their phone. | Streak as feedback: Every refill logged builds a streak. Streak loss is the only motivator stronger than convenience. | One-thumb default: Every primary action sits in the lower third of the screen. The app works on a moving train.
solution: Design the bottle into the day, and the app follows.

results.label: increase in daily active users ninety days after the redesign launched.
D7 retention — up from 11% on v1.
median time from app-open to nearest-station glance — down from 38s.
average refills logged per active user per day.

name: Terra Cork
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Cork looks cheap by default: Decades of bulletin boards and shoe insoles. The brand had to reframe cork as a premium material, not a fallback. | Sixteen product formats: Coasters, planters, trays, soap dishes, wallets, table mats, candle holders, organisers. One identity has to hold across all of them. | Sustainable without preaching: Cork is genuinely one of the most sustainable materials on earth. The brand had to communicate that without becoming an eco-lecture. | Founder-led, but not founder-fronted: Akshit didn't want his face on the brand. The material had to be the hero. Personality had to come from the product, not the founder.
strategy: Material as the hero: Every photograph leads with the cork itself — texture, grain, weight. The product is the supporting actor. | Restrained type: A single warm serif does all the typography. Cork has enough texture already. | Earth palette only: No greens, no blues. The whole brand sits in ochre, sand, terracotta, and oak — the tones cork already lives in. | Sustainability stated, not shouted: Provenance and harvest cycle printed on every label. Once. Never repeated in marketing copy.
solution: Slow material. Patient design. A thing that's still here in fifty years.

results.label: between cork harvests — the same tree, the same hands, every nine years.
average product price — premium home-goods tier.
from coaster to stool. Same material, sixteen forms.
cork bark regenerates. No tree dies for any Terra Cork product.

quote.text: The slowest material in your house. Still here in fifty years.
quote.author: Akshit Mandani

headline: Cork, finally treated like a material instead of a fix.

name: Ciao
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Italian food in India is a costume: Most Italian restaurants here use red-checkered tablecloths, Toscana fonts, and over-decorated menus. Ciao needed to feel Italian without the theatre. | Limited stock is the model, not the apology: Ciao runs out of dough by 8:30pm every night — and that's the point. The brand had to communicate scarcity as care, not failure. | Open kitchen as the brand: Watching the dough get stretched is the experience. The brand had to make the kitchen the hero — not push it to a corner. | Authentic without the lecture: Neapolitan credentials matter. But customers don't want a history lesson. The brand had to wear authenticity quietly.
strategy: Type-led, not illustrated: The whole brand is a single Italian serif and a generous grid. No fake Tuscan villas, no flag-coloured ribbons. | Olive green over red: The palette deliberately avoids Italian-flag red. Reads grown-up, not themed. | Menu as the brand surface: The single-page menu is the most-touched piece of collateral. Treated like a printed object — not a laminated leaflet. | Cap as design feature: Every printed piece names the daily dough cap. Scarcity stated, never apologised for.
solution: Ciao Pizzeria is an authentic Neapolitan wood-fired pizza joint in Ahmedabad. The pies sell out by 8:30pm every night. We built the brand so the queue makes sense.

results.label: average time the kitchen runs out of dough — every night, on purpose.
fermentation on every dough ball. Slow as a strategy.
wood-fired, imported, the bottleneck the brand makes a point of.
average wait for a Saturday-night reservation.

quote.text: Naples in Bopal. No red-checkered tablecloths. Just the dough.
quote.author: Ciao

headline: Wood-fired Naples, on a side street in Bopal.

strategy: High Visibility: Using high-contrast colors for safety and recognition. | Motion Forward: Typography and iconography that suggest forward momentum. | Functional Apparel: Designing driver gear that is actually comfortable to work in. | Clear Hierarchy: Ensuring the logo is readable from a distance at high speeds.
solution: Go Miles is rethinking urban mobility and logistics. We built a visual identity that is dynamic, reliable, and built for speed.

name: Oakmere
subtitle: ui-ux case study
problem: Conveying Craft: Online shopping lacks the tactile feedback of touching solid wood. | Shipping Logistics: Packaging needed to be robust but visually aligned with the brand. | Timeless vs Trendy: Avoiding design trends to ensure the brand feels enduring. | Detailed Specs: Presenting complex dimensions and wood types without clutter.
strategy: Honest Materials: Using natural textures in both digital and physical design. | Detail Oriented: Macro shots of joinery and wood grain. | Editorial Layouts: Treating the website like a high-end design magazine. | Quiet Confidence: Understated typography that lets the products speak.
solution: Oakmere crafts premium non-alcoholic wine. We designed a brand system and e-commerce platform that reflects the sophistication and depth of their vintage-inspired flavors without the alcohol.

name: Matcha Den
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Specialty matcha intimidates: First-timers can't tell ceremonial from culinary grade, and the ritual feels like it belongs to someone else. | Generic matcha disappoints: Most cafés serve sweetened powder mixed with milk. The drink loses the umami that makes it worth drinking. | The visual language is stuck: Matcha branding is either cartoon-kawaii or austere zen. Nothing in between feels designed for an adult who wants the real thing. | The category has no anchor: Coffee has third-wave shops to point at. Matcha doesn't. There's no Blue Bottle for tea.
strategy: Stillness: Generous whitespace. Slow type. The opposite of a third-wave coffee shop. | Vibrancy: One green that does all the lifting. No ten-shade gradients pretending to be matcha. | Ritual: Every touchpoint borrows from the whisking motion — circular, contained, repeatable. | Craft: Hand-stamped where possible. Visible imperfection. Nothing that screams CMYK.
solution: One ingredient. Whisked, not blended. Served in a room that knows the difference.

results.label: of urban tea-drinkers said matcha cafés feel either too commercial or too ceremonial.
average willingness to pay for a single ceremonial-grade matcha.
more likely to return when the space matches the drink.
discovered the brand through outdoor signage, not Instagram.

name: The Saucy Heat
subtitle: branding case study
problem: The category screams: Every chilli oil shelf is red flames, neon type, and exclamation marks. Standing out by joining the noise is impossible. | Quiet has to read as confident, not bland: Mute the noise and you risk looking like a polite condiment. The brand has to feel restrained AND serious about heat. | Bottle and tube, same brand: Bottle for kitchen, squeeze tube for picnic. The system has to feel like one brand across two very different containers. | Heat levels without scoville bars: Buyers want to know how spicy. The brand can't use the lazy pepper-icon scale everyone else uses.
strategy: Dark over bright: The whole brand sits on a near-black background. The chilli oil is the only red in the frame. | Two heat levels, named: Original and Numbing. No scales, no flames. The names do the work icons can't. | Bottle and tube, same wordmark: Identical wordmark at three sizes. Two containers, one face. | Photography in low light: Every brand asset shot under a single warm light. The oil is the brightest thing in every frame.
solution: The condiment your kitchen earns, not the one your shelf shouts about.

results.label: of repeat buyers cite 'looks like the kitchen I want' as the reason they keep reordering.
average retail — premium tier without entering luxury.
Lazada and Shopee average across 2,400 reviews.
Original and Numbing — that's the whole range. Restraint as a strategy.

quote.text: Loud sauces fade. Quiet ones get reordered.

name: Lab Coat Media
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Accessibility is usually a retrofit: Most brands and sites add accessibility at QA — colour swaps, alt-text scans, late aria-labels. That order produces worse results than designing for it from the start. | Brand and website, two timelines: Paul wanted identity and site to ship together. The visual system had to be settled before any page was laid out. | AA-clean without becoming bland: Accessibility constraints often produce visually flat brands. Lab Coat needed presence — high contrast had to feel intentional, not regulatory. | Founder-led, but enterprise-credible: Paul is the practice. The brand had to feel like a serious media operation while staying close to a single founder voice.
strategy: Contrast as composition: Every colour pair clears AA. Constraint becomes the system's rhythm — high-contrast type, generous spacing, no decorative subtlety. | Keyboard first, mouse second: Every page navigable by Tab. Focus states are designed objects, not browser defaults. | Voice on the page: Copy reads like Paul talks. Plain sentences, short paragraphs, no agency jargon. Reads aloud well on a screen reader. | One green, one black, one paper: Three colours, on purpose. Accessibility becomes the design system, not its constraint.
solution: Lab Coat Media is Paul's media practice. We designed the brand identity and the website together — built from the start around WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility and inclusivity, ensuring a seamless experience for all users rather than retrofitting it later.

results.label: every colour pair, every component, every page — by design, not by audit.
Lighthouse accessibility score at launch.
minimum contrast across every interactive element.
no focus traps, no unreachable controls, no aria-hidden-on-click hacks.

quote.text: Accessibility isn't a checklist at the end. It's a constraint at the beginning.
quote.author: Paul

headline: A media brand built to be readable by everyone.

name: Waggle
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Pet branding is for dogs: Most brands lean on cartoon paws and pet-cliché photography. The actual buyer — a human reading ingredient panels — gets nothing. | Ingredient claims vs. shelf appeal: Hero ingredients on the front of the pack matter — but most brands bury them in tiny back-panel print. | Food, treats, accessories: A kibble bag and a bandana have nothing in common physically. The brand has to feel like one company across both. | Modern, not corporate: Mass pet brands feel sterile. DTC pet brands feel hip. Waggle needed warmth without becoming a startup cliché.
strategy: Front-of-pack honesty: Protein and source named in 48pt type on the front. Buyers see the ingredient before the brand. | Illustrated, not photographed: Mascot illustration replaces stock dog photography. Owns the brand without faking another dog's photo. | Warm system: Cream base, single orange accent. Every SKU sits in the same warm palette. Shelf reads as a family. | Modular across formats: Same wordmark on a kibble bag, a bandana, and a toy. Three completely different products, one face.
solution: Real ingredients. Real bag. A dog who'd recognise the food from across the room.

results.label: of new buyers cite 'I could actually read the ingredients' as the reason for the first purchase.
average kibble bag price — premium without entering luxury.
every SKU is single-protein. No mystery meats, no fillers.
from kibble to harness. One brand, fourteen forms.

quote.text: The dog can't read the label. The human has to.
quote.author: Aanya Bose

headline: A pet brand designed for the human who actually buys it.

name: Misomaki

problem: Saturated Market: Sushi branding is notoriously repetitive. strategy: Bold Typography: A custom wordmark that commands attention without being illegible. | Stark Contrast: High-contrast palettes that make the food photography pop. | Minimal Noise: Removing every unnecessary element from the packaging. | Digital Native: Designed for screens first, print second.
solution: Misomaki redefines the modern sushi experience. In a market flooded with traditional imagery, we built a visual identity that is sharp, contemporary, and unapologetically bold.

clichéd traditional motifs used in the final identity.

name: Hardin Jewels
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Aging Demographic: The brand needed to attract younger buyers without alienating their loyal base. | Unboxing Experience: The physical packaging needed to feel as valuable as the jewelry inside. | Visual Clutter: Previous marketing was too busy. The pieces needed room to breathe. | Digital Translation: Ensuring the sparkle and detail translated perfectly to mobile screens.
strategy: Editorial Framing: Treating every product shot like a fashion editorial. | Tactile Packaging: Heavy stocks, blind embossing, and velvet interiors. | Restrained Palette: Letting the gold and gemstones provide the color. | Modern Serif: A custom logotype that bridges classic and contemporary.
solution: Hardin Jewels offers contemporary fine jewelry. We created a refined visual system anchored by a delicate monogram and subdued color palette to let the fine jewelry take center stage.

name: Evoque

problem: The Sea of Sameness: Fragrance brands often rely on the same tropes. name: Trivid Yoga
subtitle: branding case study
problem: Twenty years, no brand: Proovi had built a daily practice that drew students from four cities. There was no name above the door — just her phone number on a WhatsApp broadcast. | Online and in-studio, two faces: The in-person students and the online students were getting two different experiences. The brand had to hold both without splintering. | Tutorial library needed a brand: Selling pre-recorded yoga online is a crowded category. Proovi's twenty years of teaching is the differentiator — the brand had to surface that, not the platform. | Teacher-led, not studio-led: Most yoga brands are about the room. Trivid had to be about the teacher — without becoming a personality brand.
strategy: Teacher-first: Every brand surface leads with Proovi — not the room, not the style, not the lineage. The teacher is the differentiator. | No lotus, no sanskrit: The whole brand drops the category's default visual vocabulary. Type, colour, paper — that's the system. | Same face, two surfaces: The in-studio collateral and the online tutorial brand share one wordmark, one palette, one rhythm. | Daily, not aspirational: The brand is built around daily practice — not a weekend retreat. Voice is consistent, calm, ongoing.
solution: The teacher is the brand. Twenty years of teaching is the proof.

results.label: of daily classes — the brand's most defensible asset, finally surfaced as the headline.
Surat, Bombay, Bangalore, London, USA — where the daily online class draws regulars.
live class and tutorial library — same wordmark, two product modes.
every class is led by Proovi personally. The brand makes that the point.

name: Paperboat
subtitle: concept case study
problem: The brand is younger than the buyer: The current illustration style reads as childlike. The actual buyer is a thirty-five-year-old paying premium for nostalgia they trust. | Range is fifteen tiny stories: Every SKU has its own folktale on the back. Beautiful — but the brand has lost a single voice in favour of fifteen voices. | International shelves don't speak Hindi: Pack copy designed for a Bombay grocery doesn't read in Toronto. The brand needs a single hook that survives translation. | Nostalgia has an expiry date: The generation Paper Boat was designed for is now in their forties. The next decade of growth comes from a generation that wasn't promised these flavours.
strategy: Keep the boat, lose the diorama: The paper-boat mark stays. The crowded illustrated backgrounds go. The wordmark earns the pack on its own. | One story per range, not one per SKU: Regional clusters (summers, monsoon, festive) carry the narrative. Individual SKUs get clean, confident labels. | Heritage tones, modern weights: Existing palette stays in the family. Type weights and grid get the upgrade. | Translatable hook on every pack: A single English-Hindi cultural anchor on every pack — survives any market without becoming exoticised.
solution: The same drinks. The same memories. A brand grown up by half a decade.

results.label: of repeat buyers cite the flavour, not the packaging, as the reason they return — a brand-equity warning sign.
across the existing range — each with its own back-of-pack story.
international launch markets where the brand reads as craft, not heritage.
since founding — the longest a non-evolution can run before becoming a costume.

name: Golden Crust
subtitle: ui-ux case study
problem: Twelve years of sticker: The brand was a hand-cut sticker applied to brown bread bags. No system, no consistency, no scale. | Two bakeries, two postcodes: The original Alfama bakery and the new Príncipe Real one couldn't look like clones — but had to feel like the same family. | Bread looks bad in photos: Most bakery brands lean on stock photos of impossible loaves. Inês refused. The brand had to make her actual bread the hero. | The sticker WAS the loyalty: Customers had grown attached to the imperfect handmade sticker. Replacing it with a designed system risked losing what people loved.
strategy: Honest crust: Every photo is real bread baked that morning. No retouching, no impossible browns. | Keep the sticker spirit: The new wordmark has a hand-stamped quality. It's a system that still looks like one person made it. | Bag is the billboard: The bread bag is the most-seen surface. The whole system is tuned for the walk home. | Two sites, one rhythm: Each bakery has a slightly different signage scale. Same wordmark, different size — like siblings, not clones.
solution: The loaf was the brand for twelve years. Now they finally match.

by 11:30am, every single day of the year.

name: Royal Eats
subtitle: branding case study
problem: The food outran the brand: Five-star food, three-star packaging. Repeat customers loved it; new ones didn't know what they were looking at. | Delivery, but dressed for dining: The packaging had to survive a forty-minute ride and still feel like a gift on arrival. | Heritage without kitsch: Hyderabadi cuisine has a 500-year history. Most brands lean on Mughal silhouettes and gold. Royal Eats needed heritage without the cliché. | One identity, two rooms: The brand had to read at sixty miles an hour on a delivery bike and at six feet on a flagship facade.
strategy: Heritage, not pageantry: Reference the Nizam era without copying its ornament. The brand should feel old without looking dated. | Built for travel: Every piece of packaging is designed to look better after a forty-minute delivery ride, not worse. | One face, two rooms: The same wordmark works on a delivery sticker at three centimetres and on a façade at three metres. | Quiet luxury: No gold foil. No script flourishes. A single deep red doing all the heavy lifting.
solution: A 500-year-old cuisine, served in a brand that finally fits.

name: Plush Paws
subtitle: branding case study
role: Identity, packaging suite, retail trade dress
problem: Pet aisle = 1995 supermarket: Even premium pet brands use 2005-era pack design. Plush Paws was meant to feel like a 2026 skincare brand, just with dogs on the bag. | Five formats, one face: Cans, pouches, treat boxes, accessories, and a mobile app. The system had to feel like one brand across radically different packaging. | Affluent buyer, sceptical of premium pet: Karim's target buyer already pays premium for their own food. They've also seen pet brands inflate price without product reason. | Soft luxury, not gaudy luxury: Gold foil and crests would have been easy. The brand needed quiet luxury — confident, restrained, expensive-feeling without trying.
strategy: Restraint over decoration: No gold foil, no crests, no monogram repeats. One deep wine, one cream, one type. Quiet luxury. | Photography in low light: Every brand asset shot under a single soft light. Long shadows, soft falloff. Feels like a parfum ad. | Materials do the talking: Matte-coat substrates, debossed wordmarks, no shouting prints. The pack feels expensive in the hand. | Modular system: Can, pouch, treat box, accessory — same proportion, same wordmark, same restraint. One brand, five containers.
solution: Same restraint we'd give a luxury skincare line. Different animal.

name: Kitkat Protein Bar
subtitle: concept case study
problem: Equity, not erasure: Strip too much of the original Kit-Kat and you lose the icon. Strip too little and you look like a healthwash. | Macros are the new ingredients: Buyers read the back of the pack before the front. The macro callout has to do the work the flavour name used to. | Gym shelf, not snack aisle: The wrapper has to survive next to MyProtein, RXBAR, and Barebells. Different vocabulary, different rhythm. | Stay snackable: Functional bars are tasted, not just consumed. The brand can't forget that the original Kit-Kat is delicious.
strategy: Keep the red: The Kit-Kat red is forty percent of the brand. Lose it and you've designed a different product. | Front-of-pack honesty: Macros live where the flavour used to. No fake leaves, no athletic silhouettes. | Snap-first photography: Every shot leads with the broken bar. The product earned its photo. | Modular for SKUs: The wrapper system flexes across six flavours and three protein levels without redrawing the logo.
solution: Same break. Different reason to take it.
